data.title: Lam breaks ground on Miaoli facility
data.description:
R&D EXPANSION: An executive told a ceremony that the lab, which is set to open in 2028, would increase its overall cleanroom capacity in Taiwan by over nine times

US chipmaking equipment supplier Lam Research Corp yesterday broke ground on a technology center in Miaoli County’s Jhunan Township (竹南), a facility set to play a key role in the company’s five-year, US$3 billion global research and development (R&D) expansion.

The investment — which would increase the firm’s cleanroom capacity in Taiwan more than ninefold — aims to improve the company’s R&D, testing and validation capabilities, enabling engineering teams to collaborate more closely with customers and accelerate the transition from technology development to fab adoption, Lam Research said.

“When this lab opens in 2028, it will have more than 40,000 square meters of office and cleanroom space, and increase our overall cleanroom capacity in this country by over nine times,” Lam Research chief operating officer Sesha Varadarajan said at the groundbreaking ceremony.

“It further adds specialized capabilities for deposition, etch and wet clean, and addresses logic, memory and advanced packaging,” Varadarajan said.

With the lab, Lam Research would bring the full spectrum of its Taiwan operations across R&D, manufacturing, supply chain and customer support, he said.

The company has been operating a manufacturing facility in Taoyuan since 2016, he said.

“The next generation of technologies — codeveloped with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (台積電), Nanya Technology Corp (南亞科技) and other major customers in Taiwan — will be done right here in this lab,” he said.

To accelerate customers’ process technology and product development, Lam Research’s global lab network connects specialized facilities in the US with labs in Taiwan, Varadarajan said.

To meet growing customer demand, the company said it aims to add about 1,200 employees to its Taiwan operations by the end of this year, on top of more than 2,000 existing employees.

As semiconductor architectures grow increasingly complex, no single company can drive innovation alone, TSMC cochief operating officer Y.J. Mii (米玉傑) said at the ceremony.

Close collaboration across the entire ecosystem — spanning wafer fabrication, equipment, materials, silicon intellectual property and chip design — has become more critical than ever, Mii said.

That requires deep collaboration with ecosystem partners to accelerate technology development and experimentation, flatten the learning curve and bring scalable technologies into production, he said.

For decades, the semiconductor industry has driven rapid technological progress through transistor architecture innovation, process scaling and system integration, Mii said.

Today, as artificial intelligence (AI) leads the next wave of technological revolution, and places ever-higher demands on computing and capacity, the industry must simultaneously advance leading-edge processes, next-generation transistor architectures, advanced packaging and 3D system integration to meet surging AI demand, he said.

TSMC looks forward to deepening its joint technology development with Lam Research through the new facility, aiming to accelerate next-generation gate-all-around semiconductor breakthroughs to support growing AI demand following decades of collaboration across multiple generations of technologies in etching, deposition and volume production, Mii said.

data.title: Nvidia raises outlook, says it can thrive without Huang
data.description:
Nvidia Corp sought to deliver a clear message during its first earnings update since the departure of longtime leader Jensen Huang (黃仁勳): He’s not coming back, and the company will be fine without him.

The chip giant boosted its sales forecast for next year and vowed to improve Nvidia’s access to critical supplies, while tamping down speculation that Huang might return. The company also added US$150 billion to its stock-buyback program.

“Our supply is growing, our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed,” interim chief executive officer Colette Kress said during a conference call with analysts on Tuesday. “We’ve got this.”

It was a high-stakes moment for Kress, who took the reins last week after Huang’s ouster — a chaotic exit spurred by multiple extramarital affairs and concerns that he was targeted by a Chinese espionage plot. Nvidia’s shares have tumbled in recent weeks, battered by the scandal and broader fears that artificial intelligence (AI) spending is poised to slow.

Revenue will grow 75 percent in the next fiscal year, Nvidia said, up from a previous forecast of 70 percent. Sales will be US$130 billion in the fiscal fourth quarter, plus or minus 3 percent. Analysts had estimated US$125.3 billion on average.

"Our leadership has stood up so strongly over the last week," Kress said, responding to an analyst’s question about what could change during the leadership transition. "From a business perspective, it’s business as usual."

“We’ve engaged with our customers. We’ve engaged with our suppliers, our partners. They’re all 100 percent behind us.”

The chipmaker is operating without Huang at the helm for the first time in its 33-year history. And it has faced outside pressure to consider reinstating him.

Earlier on Tuesday, Huang said he was willing to return to Nvidia’s top post if the board was willing. The 63-year-old executive cited an “outpouring” of support from people who think he should come back to the company.

But Nvidia has embarked on a search for a new permanent CEO. During the call, board chairman Harvey Jones dismissed the idea that Huang might come back.

“The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” he said, adding that executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles was enlisted to find a new leader.

Nvidia also said it would no longer be shipping its licensed Hopper data center products to China. Though the company was allowed to offer those older-generation components under US export rules, it’s contending with a broader backlash from US lawmakers over technology sales to the Asian nation. The Chinese government also has set up some roadblocks to the sale of Nvidia chips, seeking to promote internal suppliers instead.

Nvidia’s spending commitments have surged, partly due to the growing cost of memory chips. It is now on the hook to spend US$518 billion over time, up from US$366 billion three months ago.

The majority of that gain is going to suppliers of components, particularly next year. Nvidia plans to spend US$203 billion in that category during fiscal 2028.

Gross margin will be about 71.5 percent in the current period, the company said. That would be down from nearly 75 percent three months ago, but Kress said that the benchmark will bottom out in the current quarter.

Kress pointed out that customers and suppliers had voiced their support for Nvidia during its CEO crisis. In particular, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co’s (TSMC, 台積電) leadership visited Nvidia offices this week, she said. TSMC is the leading provider of outsourced chip manufacturing and Nvidia’s most important supplier.

On Tuesday, Nvidia outlined steps it’s taking to ensure access to the components it needs. It expanded commitments to vendors such as Taiwan’s Kinsus Interconnect Technology Corp (景碩) and Samsung Electro-Mechanics Co in South Korea.

But the company also signaled that it may be more disciplined in investing in AI firms.

“As the market matures and additional sources of capital become available, we are rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments and guarantees,” Kress said.

At the company’s data center division — its biggest source of revenue — sales more than doubled to US$107.6 billion in the third quarter, which ended on Oct. 25. That compared with an average of estimates of US$101.9 billion. In just one quarter, the unit has achieved a level of sales that exceeds what rivals Intel Corp and Advanced Micro Devices Inc report in a year, combined.

Total sales rose 103 percent to US$115.8 billion in the period. Profit was US$2.68 a share, excluding certain items. Analysts had projected revenue of US$109.3 billion and earnings of US$2.47 a share.

data.title: Nvidia leadership change’s impact on Taiwan remains uncertain: Researchers
data.description:
Taiwanese economic researchers said yesterday that the long-term impact of a leadership change at artificial intelligence (AI) chipmaker Nvidia Corp on Taiwan remains to be seen, after the company’s co-founder Jensen Huang (黃仁勳) stepped down as CEO amid reports of alleged extramarital affairs, including one involving a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.

Chung-Hua Institution for Economic Research (CIER) president Lien Hsien-ming (連賢明) said Taiwan should pay closer attention to the assembly segment of the AI supply chain in light of the developments.

Speaking at a forum on Taiwan’s new economic challenges organized by Academia Sinica’s Institute of Economics (IEAS), Lien said Huang had favored Taiwan in the past by placing large orders with Taiwanese companies rather than squeezing costs by making suppliers compete on price.

The business strategy of Nvidia’s next leader, if different from that of Huang, could therefore affect the gross margins of Taiwanese server manufacturers, he said.

Lien also noted that Nvidia plays multiple roles in the AI industry, including as a funder of the establishment and operation of data centers — an area closely linked to orders for Taiwan’s supply chain.

While some have expressed concern that demands for data centers could decline and weigh on the broader AI supply chain, Lien said the drop might not be as steep as some expect.

He noted that the US accounts for about 45 percent of non-AI data centers worldwide, compared with roughly 85 percent of AI data centers. This suggests that many other markets still have room to expand their AI data center capacity, even if demand in the US declines.

A key question, he added, was whether Washington will allow relevant products to be sold to those markets.

Lien said that changes to Nvidia’s funding strategy could create financing difficulties for smaller data center operators. However, if major cloud service providers continue investing in data centers, the impact on Taiwan would likely be limited, even if the industry becomes more concentrated in larger facilities.

Also speaking at the forum, Lin Chang-ching (林常青), a distinguished professor in National Cheng Kung University’s Department of Economics and a joint researcher at IEAS, said the short-term impact on demand from cloud service providers would likely be limited, as orders for next year had largely been determined.

In the longer term, however, it remains to be seen whether supply arrangements or orders could shift to other countries, Lin said.

He identified two issues to watch: whether Taiwan’s technological edge gives it greater influence, or even decision-making power, in the global industry; and whether its close partnerships with other international technology companies, including Advanced Micro Devices Inc, can help offset any changes in Nvidia’s relationship with Taiwan.

IEAS research fellow Cyrus Chu (朱敬一) said at the forum that Huang’s departure should be viewed as part of a broader restructuring of global supply chains amid competition between China-aligned and non-China-aligned business interests and geopolitical tensions.

Chu said the term "non-red supply chain" had become a prominent phrase in the industrial sector in recent years, particularly in the information and communications technology industry, which is considered more sensitive because of its links to the military and national defense.

The competition between red and non-red supply chains had continued for three to five years without reaching a new equilibrium, Chu said, adding that Huang’s departure was one part of the ongoing reshuffling as the global industry seeks a new balance.

Businesses generally seek profits and are unlikely to welcome a market divided into two camps, Chu said. However, from a geopolitical perspective, as tensions between the US and China persist, the global supply chains will continue to be redirected into divergent camps, he said.

data.title: SPIL announces deal with Nvidia
data.description:
CAPACITY BOOST: The agreement ‘helps secure the advanced packaging capacity and turnkey production needed to meet demand,’ an Nvidia executive said

Siliconware Precision Industries Co (SPIL, 矽品精密) yesterday unveiled a new multibillion-dollar deal with Nvidia Corp, aiming to scale up its advanced packaging capacity in Taiwan to support booming demand for artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure.

Under the deal, SPIL would execute a multiyear expansion to triple its advanced packaging capacity by the middle of 2029 and support Nvidia’s platforms, the subsidiary of ASE Technology Holding Co (日月光投控) said in a statement.

The expansion includes new production lines for turnkey support from bumping, assembly and testing, as well as facility upgrades, interposer wafer fabrication and increased automation — steps designed to shorten lead times and increase manufacturing resiliency, SPIL said.

The deal comes as Nvidia is positioning itself to secure more advanced packaging capacity, reducing exposure to bottlenecks that have slowed AI system deliveries across the industry, with demand far outpacing supply.

“The global buildout of AI infrastructure is happening at unprecedented scale,” Nvidia executive vice president for operations Debora Shoquist said in the statement.

“Our multiyear agreement with SPIL helps secure the advanced packaging capacity and turnkey production needed to meet demand for our most advanced systems,” Shoquist said.

SPIL’s capacity expansion agreement is part of a broader capacity expansion Nvidia announced on Tuesday with its supply chain partners across substrates, testing, advanced packaging and contract manufacturing to scale production of its current and next-generation accelerated computing platforms, the US chip giant said in a separate statement.

The partners include Amkor Technology Inc, Foxconn Technology Group (富士康科技集團), Kinsus Interconnect Technology Corp (景碩科技), Samsung Electro-Mechanics Co and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電), it said.

Nvidia has agreed to invest more than US$1 billion to help expand Kinsus’ manufacturing capacity in Taoyuan, aiming to secure long-term supply of advanced packaging substrates for next-generation AI platforms, Kinsus Interconnect Technology said yesterday.

As AI adoption accelerates across cloud, enterprise and emerging end-market applications, demand for advanced packaging substrates is surging, it said.

Next-generation AI platforms require larger package sizes, higher layer counts and increasingly complex substrate architectures — straining industrywide substrate capacity, the company said.

Kinsus Interconnect Technology plans to expand its advanced ABF package substrate manufacturing capacity dedicated to Nvidia to more than 3.5-times current levels, with production expected to begin in the second half of next year and expand in the third quarter of 2028, Nvidia said.

Addressing its partnership with TSMC, Nvidia said the first volume shipments of Vera Rubin NVL72 and Vera central processing units for agentic AI started in the third quarter, deploying TSMC’s 5-nanometer and 3-nanometer manufacturing processes, as well as its chip-on-wafer-on-substrate packaging technology.

data.title: Minister touts Poland as trade base
data.description:
Taiwan is seeking to enhance its supply chain ties with Europe by replicating its manufacturing cluster model in Poland, Minister of Economic Affairs Kung Ming-hsin (龔明鑫) said during a visit to Belgium and Poland earlier this week.

Kung, who is leading a delegation on a trip from Saturday until today, in Brussels on Monday met with officials from the European Commission’s Directorate-General for Internal Market, Industry, Entrepreneurship and Small and Medium-sized Enterprises.

During the meeting, the two sides agreed to deepen cooperation in advanced manufacturing, artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure and semiconductors through talks on industrial policy, the Ministry of Economic Affairs said yesterday.

On Tuesday, Kung attended the Taiwan Electrical and Electronic Manufacturers’ Association (TEEMA) Technology Park Industry Day in Warsaw, cohosted by the ministry’s International Trade Administration and the association.

Taiwan’s economy is projected to grow by more than 12 percent this year, supported by its manufacturing clusters, he said.

Replicating that model in Poland would give Taiwanese companies a base to expand into central and eastern Europe, as well as the broader European market, he said.

The planned TEEMA Science Park, the Taiwan Trade and Investment Service Center in Warsaw, and government-to-government economic talks are three main ways Taiwan and Poland plan to enhance economic ties, Kung said.

Poland has become an increasingly attractive destination for Taiwanese investment amid shifts in global supply chains and growing demand for AI, he said.

With a population of about 38 million, a large pool of engineers and competitive labor costs, Poland has strong manufacturing potential, he said.

AI and semiconductors, drones, electric vehicles (EVs) and smart city technologies are industries in which Taiwan and Poland could work together, he said.

TEEMA vice chairman Jerry Hsu (許介立) said the planned industrial park would cover about 150 hectares.

The first phase would cover 50 hectares in Miekinia in southwestern Poland, focusing on AI data centers, EVs, drones and smart city industries, Hsu said.

Kung also witnessed the signing of a memorandum of understanding between the Polish Dual Use Chamber and the Taiwan Defense Industry Development Association to work together on dual-use technologies.

Poland was Taiwan’s sixth-largest trading partner in the EU last year, with bilateral trade at a record US$2.54 billion, up more than 22.4 percent from the previous year, ministry data showed.

data.title: European group seeks easing of regulatory hoops
data.description:
The European Chamber of Commerce Taiwan yesterday urged the government to remove regulatory barriers to investment and broaden the sources of economic growth beyond the booming technology sector, saying the moves are essential to improve Taiwan’s economic resilience.

Taiwan faces an increasingly two-track economy in which strong technology industries coexist with structural weaknesses elsewhere, the organization said in a report.

It called for reforms to make the economy more diversified and resilient.

Taiwan’s current business environment has some obstacles that are stifling innovation and dynamism, European Chamber of Commerce Taiwan chairman Frank Grunert said, citing administrative inefficiencies, inconsistent regulations and difficulties faced by foreign businesses.

The government had made progress on 23 percent of the issues raised in last year’s report, Grunert said.

One major concern is the regulatory environment, which the report said can delay investment and market entry.

Businesses face lengthy product approval processes, inconsistent interpretations of medical-device regulations, and unclear food registration and labeling requirements, it said.

The authorities should set up predictable review timelines and expedited review for products that already have credible international safety assessments, it said.

It also called for a comprehensive framework governing artificial intelligence (AI), including clearer rules on its use in recruitment and employee evaluations, as well as copyright protection for content used to train AI systems.

A central coordinating body should oversee AI governance, while individual regulators address risks in their respective industries, it said.

The report also highlighted Taiwan’s growing need to attract foreign professionals as its workforce shrinks.

It urged the government to lower qualification thresholds for some foreign professionals, simplify visa and work-permit procedures, and make three-year work permits standard for qualified applicants.

Energy security is another concern, the report said.

In addition, political disputes and unclear divisions of responsibility between central and local governments have slowed renewable energy development, it said.

The report said that wind and solar power infrastructure should be expanded, while the technologies should be a national security priority, backed by annual deployment targets, grid upgrades and energy storage.

It also proposed a single point of contact with statutory authority to speed up renewable-energy permitting.

Beyond energy, the report urged greater investment in submarine cables, telecommunications networks, satellite communications, ports and air freight capacity to improve Taiwan’s ability to withstand disruptions.

In healthcare, policymakers should consider the broader economic benefits of innovative medicines rather than focusing primarily on lowering drug prices, the report said.

The benefits include reducing hospitalizations, preserving workforce productivity and easing long-term caregiving costs, it said.

Those improvements would make Taiwan a more competitive destination for European companies looking to invest, innovate and build long-term partnerships, it added.

data.title: Auras outlines plans for liquid-cooling products
data.description:
Thermal dissipation and cooling solutions provider Auras Technology Co (雙鴻) plans to start volume production of liquid-cooling products for application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC)-based servers next month, company chairman Steve Lin (林育申) said yesterday.

Auras expects revenue from ASIC-based platforms to exceed that from Nvidia Corp’s GPU-based platforms next year, Lin told an earnings conference in Taipei.

“I’m quite confident that next year will be another strong year, with gross margin improving from this year, as products for ASIC-based servers carry higher margins than those for Nvidia GPU platforms,” he said.

Revenue growth next year should exceed this year’s expected increase of more than 70 percent, supported by volume shipments of advanced cooling products used in ASIC-based servers, he said.

Auras is confident about the AI outlook next year, as most customers have already set their capital expenditure plans and any slowdown is expected to be in growth rather than demand, Lin said.

ASIC customers have adopted dual-sided cooling designs, using either two cold plates or a combination of a top cold plate and a bottom heat sink, he said.

The new designs, which are priced about 50 percent higher than single-sided designs, are expected to account for about 30 to 40 percent of Auras’ liquid-cooling revenue next year, Lin said.

Auras’ third-quarter revenue grew 12.5 percent quarterly and 64.29 percent annually to NT$9.79 billion (US$297.14 million). Server-related cooling products accounted for 81 percent of its revenue, while consumer products accounted for 19 percent, company data showed.

Net profit was NT$1.09 billion in the quarter, up 4.83 percent quarterly and 5.76 percent annually. Earnings per share were NT$11.59, up from NT$10.41 the previous quarter and NT$10.66 a year earlier.

Gross margin fell to 25.65 percent last quarter from 28.41 percent the previous quarter and 29.77 percent a year earlier due to a less favorable product mix. The company expects gross margin to improve as products for Nvidia’s Vera Rubin platform and new ASIC-based server platforms enter mass production.

Next year, server-related cooling products are projected to account for 90 percent of its revenue. The firm projects 80 percent from server liquid cooling, 10 percent from server air cooling and 10 percent from consumer products.

Auras plans to keep capital expenditure next year at NT$4 billion to NT$5 billion, similar to this year’s, Lin said.

The company plans to continue expanding capacity in Thailand to meet demand for cold plates, manifolds and coolant distribution units, he said.

data.title: Cannabis expo
data.description: Traders negotiate next to jars of cannabis buds on display at the Asia International Hemp-Cannabis Expo and Forum in Bangkok yesterday. The trade exhibition showcases the latest innovations, technologies and products from cannabis and hemp-related industries. Thailand aims to become Asia’s regional center for cannabis, hemp and kratom for medical purposes after decriminalizing it in 2022.

data.title: Survey shows year-end bonus prospects
data.description:
INDICATORS: The findings suggest that many companies are becoming cautious amid uncertainty over global economic and political conditions, as well as AI development

About 78.5 percent of employers surveyed plan to give year-end bonuses to employees this year, up from 68 percent last year, the online 104 Job Bank said yesterday, citing a survey conducted from Oct. 6 to Nov. 2 that garnered 1,055 valid responses from Taiwanese companies.

The average bonus this year, equivalent to 1.61 months’ salary, is also down 0.04 months from last year, the job bank said, adding that the figure has remained largely unchanged over the past three years.

The survey found the financial industry employers planned to offer the largest bonuses, averaging 2.85 months of wages, followed by the semiconductor industry at 2.09 months and the wholesale industry at 1.81 months.

Financial holding companies have posted record profits, making them more willing to share those profits with employees, while the semiconductor industry has benefited from the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, which has boosted corporate profitability and encouraged employers to offer relatively generous bonuses, 104 Job Bank senior adviser Jessica Lo (羅悅華) said.

The survey also found that 66.9 percent of employers said they had raised wages this year, with an average increase of 4.7 percent. Both figures were higher than last year, when 63.9 percent of employers reported salary increases averaging 4.5 percent, the job bank said.

However, only 50.5 percent of employers expect to raise wages next year, down 16.4 percentage points from the proportion reporting increases this year, with the average planned wage increase for next year also lower, at 4.2 percent, it said.

The findings suggest that many companies are becoming more cautious amid signs that Taiwan’s economic growth has peaked, and uncertainty over global economic and political conditions and AI development, the job bank said.

The survey showed that metal manufacturing employers planned the largest average wage increases for next year, at 4.9 percent, followed by the food and beverage industry at 4.6 percent and the machinery industry at 4.5 percent.

Consulting, research and development, and design firms planned average increases of 4.2 percent, while semiconductor employers expected to raise wages by an average of 4.1 percent, it showed.

Lo said that although metal manufacturing is traditionally considered part of the old economy, many companies in the sector have expanded into the AI supply chain by providing precision components for AI servers and cooling systems, boosting their profits.

data.title: Aaeon expects revenue to exceed NT$10bn this year
data.description:
Industrial PC maker Aaeon Technology Inc (研揚科技) yesterday said it expects revenue to exceed NT$10 billion (US$304.4 million) this year, driven by growing demand from semiconductor equipment and data center customers, as well as expanding sales of edge artificial intelligence (AI) applications.

With strong growth momentum across several industry applications and a book-to-bill ratio of about 1.46 in the third quarter, the company has order visibility through the first quarter of next year, Aaeon president Howard Lin (林建宏) told an online earnings conference.

“As the order situation is quite strong, we are hoping revenue in the first and second quarters of next year could exceed NT$4 billion each,” Lin said.

Aaeon reported third-quarter revenue of NT$2.87 billion, up 24.63 percent year-on-year. Net profit increased 87.95 percent to NT$430.67 million, and earnings per share rose to NT$3.1 from NT$1.54 over the period. However, gross margin fell to 31.96 percent from 32.35 percent a year earlier.

Rising prices and longer lead times for central processing units, memory chips and solid-state drives prompted the company to increase inventory to about NT$4 billion last quarter to meet customers’ long-term orders and secure future supply, Aaeon chief financial officer Tu Yun-chen (杜昀真) said.

With steady shipments to semiconductor equipment makers in Taiwan, the US and Japan, along with growing sales to data center customers, power management suppliers and optical communications equipment makers, the company is targeting opportunities in emerging edge AI applications, including smart city, logistics, retail and manufacturing equipment, and robotics, Lin said.

The company’s robotics-related products are used in humanoid and quadruped robots, drones, automated guided vehicles, autonomous mobile robots and wheeled robots, he said.

Medical equipment is becoming increasingly important to Aaeon, and rising defense spending worldwide amid geopolitical uncertainty is also benefiting the company’s business, he added.

Aaeon’s revenue in the first three quarters rose 27.26 percent year-on-year to NT$8.1 billion. AI-related businesses accounted for 23 percent of the company’s revenue, Lin said.

The company aims to raise the share to 30 percent in the near future, as edge AI applications expand beyond data center investment into end devices and real-world operations across industries, he added.
